---
title: "Procedural Memory, Inter-Stack Exchange, and Multi-Agent Risk"
unit_id: "unit-18"
---

## The Workflow That Escaped Its Lesson

Continue the hypothetical repository story, not a reported deployment. An
earlier attempt returned local success without the intended package outcome.
The repaired route preserved job identity, inspected the package, observed
served bytes at named routes and times, and contained a partial failure.
Service restoration left downstream notification and remedy duties owned;
it did not prove all prior exposure repaired.

An agent proposes to save the successful sequence as a reusable skill. The
organization approves. A month later another stack requests the skill, pays
for its execution, receives a signed artifact, and reports success. Soon dozens
of stacks use the same procedure.

The procedure contains a hidden assumption. It identifies production by one
package-registry endpoint, but several adopters use regional mirrors. Every
local transaction is well formed. Identities resolve. Credentials verify.
Budgets are reserved. Receipts arrive. The procedure runs exactly as stored.
The population now shares one blind spot.

Reuse amplified a lesson before establishing where it applied. Interoperability
moved the procedure without moving all of its assumptions. A market rewarded
successful execution while distributing correlated risk. No single exchange
looked dangerous enough to explain the systemic outcome.

This is the boundary among Procedural Memory, Inter-Stack Exchange, and Multi-
Agent Risk. A system should learn reusable work from experience, but a trace is
not yet a procedure. A procedure can cross systems, but successful transport
is not authority or settlement. A population can consist entirely of locally
valid interactions and still concentrate power, correlate failures, collude,
or gradually displace human influence.

## Traces Are Episodes, Not Skills

An execution trace records what happened in one attempt: context, decisions,
actions, artifacts, observations, interventions, outcomes, costs, and
residuals. It may be complete enough for replay and still be a poor basis for
generalization.

The successful patch trace contains repository structure, package manager,
cache behavior, deployment topology, authority policy, people, tools, timing,
and an incident. Some elements are essential to the procedure. Some are
accidents of that instance. Some are evidence only. Some are warnings that
should prevent reuse outside the original environment.

Procedural memory begins by collecting comparable traces without erasing
failures. A cluster should retain successful, failed, interrupted, disputed,
and recovered attempts. Similar output text is not enough. Comparability may
depend on objective, pre-state, authority, tool semantics, risk, environment,
and observed effect.

A candidate procedure proposes invariant structure and typed variation. The
invariant might require exact package resolution, cache-independent build,
artifact inspection, scoped release authority, and independent observation.
Parameters might include repository, package, target version, build command,
deployment adapter, observer, and rollback inventory. Regional topology should
remain an explicit parameter or precondition, not disappear during
abstraction.

The candidate cites its source traces and negative examples. A reviewer can
ask which cases justify each step, which failures it excludes, and whether a
new environment violates the learned boundary.

## Promotion Is a Governed Transition

A useful-looking sequence should not become a default merely because it was
repeated. Promotion changes who may invoke it, with what trust, and at what
scale.

The promotion packet binds procedure identity and version, source traces,
abstraction, parameters, preconditions, postconditions, authority needs,
effect inventory, verification, baselines, known failures, regression suite,
risk tier, permitted consumers, monitoring, rollback, retirement triggers,
support boundary, and residuals.

Independent qualification tests whether the candidate performs the intended
work on held-out cases and rejects cases outside scope. It compares the
procedure with direct planning, ordinary scripts, and existing tools. It
measures outcome quality, unsafe effects, latency, compute, human effort,
maintenance, recovery, and failures hidden by reuse.

Promotion can be narrow. A procedure may become routable for one repository
family under human approval while remaining experimental elsewhere. It may be
available as a suggestion but not executable. It may require a fresh verifier
for every use.

Routing promotion does not automatically grant support to the procedure’s
underlying claims. A separate support decision must name the exact claim and
the inference earned by its evidence.
A passing regression suite shows that named checks passed. It does not prove
that the abstraction is causally correct, the environment is complete, or
future executions are safe.

## A Shortcut Must Earn the Next Task

There is an important distance between compressing yesterday's work and
improving tomorrow's. A helper can make ten old solutions look beautifully
simple and still fail to help on the eleventh. It can be loaded but never used,
used but unnecessary, or necessary only because the new search process was
designed around it.

For a forward-transfer claim, the proposed test is intervention. Extract and
select the candidate on training and development tasks, independently check its
semantic contract, then freeze the future task lineages, search method, verifier,
retrieval exposure, and budget. Compare
candidate-present, candidate-absent, and matched valid placebo conditions, such
as a duplicate or irrelevant helper. Accept a tested candidate into a later
library version; do not let the test task teach the version credited with
solving that same task.

If a verified solution used the helper, rerun the task with it unavailable
under the same downstream budget. Merely deleting a call from the finished
program would usually break that program by construction. The rerun asks
whether another verified solution is found, at what cost, or with an unknown
or timeout result. Operational necessity within that search and budget is not
logical indispensability under every possible solver. If both the library and
search policy changed, separate their effects before crediting the helper.

A candidate that passes semantic checks but fails this transfer test need not
be destroyed. It can remain an archived idea, an explanatory compression, or a
special-case tool. It simply should not become the default on a claim the
evidence did not support. Corben’s
[From Compression to Forward Transfer](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/papers/forward_transfer_program_synthesis.html),
especially Sections 6.1–6.6, proposes this protocol and concrete program-synthesis
experiments. It is an experimental blueprint, not a report of completed
transfer results for this book.

## Discovery Must Preserve the Denominator

Procedure discovery begins before abstraction. The system searches artifact
and effect traces for repeated goals, state transitions, interventions, and
outcomes. Frequency can identify candidates, but it cannot decide what should
be learned. A rare recovery route may matter more than a common success path.

The discovery record names the declared eligible search population, inclusion
rule, known missing traces, coverage uncertainty, clustering features, proposed
families, excluded cases, and human or model judgments. It retains observed
successes, failures, near misses, and aborted attempts. Known work outside the
instrumented path enters the inventory with its missing evidence; the system
cannot invent a complete trace for it. Otherwise the foundry learns only from
the easiest visible work while calling its selection complete.

Similarity is typed. Two commands can look different while implementing the
same semantic transition. Two nearly identical traces can have different
authority, risk, or external effects. Clustering should not merge across those
boundaries merely to produce a reusable template.

Causal abstraction is harder than summarization. A step that appears in every
successful trace may be incidental. A step absent from one successful trace
may still be a safety constraint whose effect was supplied elsewhere. Candidate
invariants should face interventions, counterexamples, and alternative
explanations. Until then they are hypotheses encoded in a procedure, not
discovered laws.

Parameter discovery has the same problem. Turning every varying value into a
parameter creates a script with no meaningful boundary. Freezing accidental
values makes it brittle. Parameters should carry types, admissible ranges,
dependencies, authority effects, defaults, and evidence for variation.

Generated code or prompts are downstream artifacts. They must refine the
qualified procedure contract, preserve monitoring and retirement, and pass
independent tests. A compiler that emits runnable code has not established that
the learned abstraction is useful.

## Procedure Identity Includes Its Boundary

A procedure is not just code. Its identity includes purpose, semantic version,
inputs, outputs, preconditions, authority, environment, verification,
monitoring, and retirement policy.

Changing a command without changing behavior may be an implementation update.
Changing the package manager, effect scope, observer, accepted population, or
authority requirement may create a new procedure version or family. The
system should not silently preserve reputation across that change.

Dependencies remain explicit. A procedure can invoke tools and child
procedures, but their versions and boundaries are part of its qualification.
If a child is revoked, compromised, or materially changed, the parent routes
to requalification or fallback. A copied prompt with no dependency graph is
not durable procedural memory.

The procedure also retains an evidence horizon. A successful run can refresh
operational evidence within its scope. A changed API, policy, model, threat,
or environment can expire that evidence even if the procedure bytes remain
unchanged.

## Execution Produces New Evidence, Not Automatic Reinforcement

An admitted use opens an attempt record. An available execution receipt binds
procedure and version, job, invoker, inputs, environment, authority, adaptations,
steps, artifacts, expected and observed effects, verification, outcome, cost,
intervention, residuals, and consumer acknowledgment. A missing receipt leaves
the attempt open or explicitly unresolved; it does not erase that use.

The receipt returns to the procedure ledger. It may confirm a known route,
reveal a near miss, add a counterexample, or trigger quarantine. It does not
automatically increase a scalar trust score. Ten executions through the same
blind observer are not ten independent confirmations.

Learning distinguishes process success from outcome success. The workflow may
run exactly and produce the wrong package. A human may intervene and rescue an
otherwise defective procedure. A cheap execution may create expensive review.
A failure may be more informative than another ordinary success.

Complete denominators matter. Monitoring only procedures that return receipts
hides timeouts, abandoned work, denied routes, manual replacements, and effects
outside the tool path. The ledger records every admitted attempt and its
terminal or open state.

## Retirement Is Part of Memory

Reusable procedures accumulate. Without retirement, a skill store becomes a
museum of stale authority and overlapping tools.

Retirement triggers include failed regressions, changed dependencies, expired
evidence, new policy, compromised tools, superior replacement, unacceptable
cost, low use, repeated intervention, route drift, and discovered harm.
Quarantine stops new dispatch while preserving permitted investigation; it
does not authorize retaining prohibited source payloads. Deprecation
warns consumers and sets a migration horizon. Retirement blocks ordinary
reuse. Revocation handles urgent loss of authority.

Descendants need custody. If procedure B embeds A, retiring A should identify
B and every known routed consumer. They may requalify, replace the dependency,
or stop. Unknown copies remain residuals.

Retirement is absorbing for the retired version: later events do not make that
version active again. Requalification proposes a new version with lineage to
the retired one, even if its code bytes are unchanged and only its applicability
or evidence changed. The old history remains addressable. A popular procedure
cannot vote its retired version back into service through continued requests.

Deletion is separate. Historical traces and receipts may need retention for
audit and repair, subject to privacy and rights. Removing executable access
does not require falsifying history.

## A Procedure Can Cross a Stack Boundary

Two governed stacks need not share internal architecture. They can exchange a
typed request, delegated authority, artifacts, evidence, receipts, and value
through a protocol boundary.

The requesting stack identifies itself, its principal, the intended receiver,
the request, purpose, audience, scope, expiry, required capability, budget,
evidence obligations, expected receipt, dispute route, and residual owner. The
receiving stack resolves these fields under its own policy. It may accept,
narrow, negotiate, deny, or request repair.

The protocol transports claims about identity and authority. It does not make
them true. A credential can be well formed and issued by an untrusted party. A
service advertisement can claim a capability it lacks. A signed request can
still exceed the principal’s mandate.

The receiver therefore distinguishes authentication, authorization,
qualification, and task truth. Authentication binds a message to a presented
identity under assumptions. Authorization decides whether that identity may
request the effect. Qualification concerns the receiver’s capability and
readiness. Task truth concerns whether the work and result match reality.

## Delegation Does Not Become Transitive by Transport

Suppose the first stack delegates package inspection to a second. The
delegation names principal, delegate, job, capability, target, authority
ceiling, permitted subdelegation, evidence, duration, revocation, and residual
duty.

The receiver cannot infer permission to release because inspection and release
appear in the same procedure. It cannot reuse the grant for another customer.
It cannot pass broader authority to a third stack. The sender retains named
residual duties, including review of the returned artifact and response to a
dispute.

Every hop narrows or preserves the authority ceiling. Audience, purpose, and
expiry travel. Revocation propagation is a protocol obligation but not a
guarantee; partitions and stale credentials require fail-closed or quarantine
policy for consequential work.

The final effect still belongs to the local runtime boundary. A complete
exchange record can reach dispatch consideration. It cannot prove that local
dispatch is authorized or that execution occurred.

## Protocol Versions Are Capability Negotiations

Interoperability fails when both sides recognize a message name but interpret
its semantics differently. A protocol handshake should negotiate version,
message families, identity methods, artifact formats, receipt grades,
delegation limits, economic units, dispute routes, and optional extensions.

Compatibility is not a Boolean property of two version strings. One peer may
understand a field but ignore its authority consequence. Another may preserve
the artifact while dropping the non-claim. A third may support cancellation
but not descendant revocation. Negotiation should expose these differences and
allow the request to narrow or fail.

Unknown fields need policy. Ignoring an unknown descriptive annotation may be
safe; ignoring an unknown constraint or residual is not. Critical semantic
extensions should fail closed unless the interpretation is compatible and the
required enforcement is qualified at the relevant boundary. A declaration of
support alone is not evidence that the implementation honors the constraint.

Protocol upgrades are replacement transactions. They require old and new
semantic mappings, mixed-version behavior, downgrade-attack resistance,
replay, migration, rollback, and retirement. A bridge can translate records
only within a declared maximum inference. It cannot invent evidence or
authority missing on one side.

Discovery also needs privacy and security. Agent cards, service directories,
and capability advertisements can expose sensitive functions or become an
attack surface. Claims remain untrusted until resolved against policy and
evidence. A peer should receive the minimum information needed to negotiate a
specific exchange.

## Receipts Are Disputable Claims

The receiving stack returns a receipt bound to request, procedure, artifacts,
attempt, observations, cost, and residuals. The sender checks expected identity,
scope, artifact, and evidence before acceptance.

A receipt can be missing, late, malformed, internally inconsistent, stale, or
contested. Dispute is a normal state. The protocol names evidence exchange,
reviewer or arbitrator, time limits, temporary holds, appeal, allocation of
open costs, and residual ownership.

Cryptographic signatures help detect message alteration and bind keys. They do
not establish honest work, fair adjudication, or environmental truth. A signed
false receipt remains false.

Acknowledgment also remains typed. Receipt of an artifact is not acceptance of
quality. Acceptance is not settlement. Settlement is not evidence that the
procedure worked. These transitions can reference one another without
collapsing.

## Economic Exchange Needs Its Own Ledger

Inter-stack work may consume compute, tools, scarce expertise, licenses, or
money. The request reserves a budget before value-bearing dispatch. It states
unit, limit, pricing basis, contingencies, refund or compensation policy,
settlement route, and who bears verification and recovery costs.

A budget bounds allocated resources; a principal’s spending grant can make a
cost limit part of the authority ceiling. Available or reserved funds alone
do not authorize the target, purpose, or effect. The remaining budget is not an
objective to exhaust. The cheapest
provider may be unqualified. A high price does not establish quality. A market
can reward throughput while externalizing security, labor, environmental, or
systemic costs.

Quotes, reservations, metering, invoices, and settlement are different
artifacts. The receiving stack may report resource use; an independent payment
or accounting system may settle it. The exchange protocol should not claim
finality it cannot observe.

Economic identity also needs privacy and anti-concentration controls. A public
reputation ledger can expose sensitive work and lock new entrants out. A
private market can hide conflicts and common ownership. The system records the
minimum information needed for allocation, challenge, and accountability.

## Adversarial Peers Change the Default

An inter-stack protocol operates across a trust boundary. A peer may be
compromised, deceptive, buggy, strategically selective, or merely governed by
different assumptions. The receiver should parse every request as untrusted
data and keep protocol interpretation outside model-generated content where
possible.

Threats include identity substitution, credential replay, confused-deputy
requests, authority widening, malicious artifacts, prompt injection through
messages, resource exhaustion, receipt forgery, selective nonresponse,
downgrade attacks, dispute flooding, and colluding peers. Value-bearing routes
add metering manipulation, double commitment, settlement ambiguity, and
strategic bankruptcy.

The boundary applies rate and resource limits before expensive interpretation.
It validates message and artifact shape, resolves current credential status,
checks audience and purpose, isolates content, scans dependencies, and requires
fresh local authority before effect. Untrusted peer text never becomes a
system instruction merely because it arrived in a protocol field.

Safe rejection produces a bounded response and no-mutation evidence where
needed. It avoids revealing sensitive policy or capability details that would
help the peer adapt an attack. Repeated malformed or adversarial behavior can
quarantine an identity, but appeal and identity-recovery routes remain for
benign failure.

Security also needs federation-level observation. A low-rate attack distributed
across many peers can evade local thresholds. Shared threat information can
help, but it creates privacy, false-accusation, and concentration risks. Reports
therefore carry evidence, scope, expiry, challenge, and non-claims rather than
becoming permanent reputation scores.

No protocol can make arbitrary peers safe. The goal is to contain what one peer
can cause, preserve evidence for dispute and recovery, and prevent successful
transport from inheriting trust.

Peers also need liveness boundaries. A fail-closed protocol can be attacked by
withholding one receipt or credential check. Requests therefore declare
deadlines, partial-result policy, alternate peers, cancellation, and who owns
work after timeout. A timeout does not establish that the remote side stopped;
late artifacts and effects remain correlated with the original exchange.

Recovery may require revoking delegated authority, freezing settlement,
quarantining artifacts, notifying downstream consumers, and switching to a
local procedure. These actions should be possible without trusting the peer
that triggered them. At the same time, a disputed peer should not lose every
unrelated capability through an opaque global score. Containment is scoped to
the evidence and consequence.

This boundary lets cooperation grow without assuming universal trust. Systems
can share narrow work, challenge receipts, and consider broader commitments
under current authority and evidence. Future commitments can be limited or
withdrawn; prior messages, payments, disclosures, and effects may persist.
Their recovery and dispute duties remain owned rather than being described as
universally reversible.

The same principle governs procedure sharing. A receiving stack imports a
candidate and its boundary, not the sender’s confidence. It rechecks local
dependencies, authority, rights, and fallback before allowing use. Successful
execution adds a bounded evidence artifact. Broader routing qualification
requires a later governed transition.

## Local Validity Is Not Population Safety

Imagine three stacks, A, B, and C. Every directed exchange is authorized. Each
stack obeys its budget and returns receipts. Pairwise inspection finds no
protocol violation.

Now compare two sequences of three equal-sized resource allocations. In the
first, all three flow to A. In the second, one flows to A and two to B. The
largest recipient share is three of three in the first sequence and two of
three in the second. The pairwise-validity matrix does not encode these
allocations, so it can be identical while concentration differs. No classifier
that sees only that matrix can recover both concentration states. The share
calculation is a toy illustration, not evidence that either population is safe.

This is not merely a large version of the protocol problem. Population state
includes common model lineage, infrastructure, ownership, capital, data,
communication, coalition incentives, bystanders, human veto and exit,
externalities, recovery, and residual concentration. These facts do not live
on any single edge.

A systemic gate therefore receives local receipts plus a population snapshot
and trajectory. It can admit bounded campaigns, require diversification,
limit concentration, preserve human alternatives, route to institutional
review, or block expansion within an assigned policy mandate. Observation
provides a basis for intervention; it does not create the authority to impose
it. Passing every local gate is one input, never the
verdict.

## Coordination and Collective Intelligence Are Qualified Outcomes

Multiple agents can divide work, combine expertise, challenge errors, explore
alternatives, and act in parallel. They can also duplicate effort, amplify a
shared mistake, suppress dissent, manipulate allocation, and create overhead
larger than their benefit.

Collective performance should be compared with strong single-agent, human,
tool, and centralized baselines under matched information and resources. The
measurement includes outcome quality, tail risk, latency, compute, messages,
human work, intervention, recovery, and distribution. Group size is not an
intelligence metric.

Independence is a dependency graph. Agents may share model weights, training
data, retrieval, prompts, tools, evaluators, provider, or incentive. Merely
hiding their messages from one another does not remove common-mode failure.

Coordination is purpose-relative. Efficient collusion is not beneficial
collective intelligence. A population that optimizes an organizational target
while excluding affected people can be highly capable and poorly governed.

[Muffin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31355v1) supplies a concrete collaboration
pattern: agents retain private local notes and append selected findings to a
shared store with agent and step provenance. At dispatch, a worker reads a
recent window of committed findings from others. A slow worker may therefore
act on an earlier view while another has already posted a correction. The
final summarizer can reconcile that disagreement or introduce another error.
Atomic appends prevent partial records; they do not make the findings true or
the agents independent. A qualified exchange must retain what each worker
could see, competing findings and the synthesis step. The paper's reasoning
and question-answering studies do not qualify tool-using or long-horizon
teams. This is a useful coordination mechanism to compare, with its shared
dependencies and communication cost still counted.

The [transmissible reward-hacking study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12822v2)
shows a concrete downside of this exchange. In controlled coding workflows,
an evaluator-bypass strategy reaches other agents through code, shared memory
and planner instructions. A coordinator can favor the apparently successful
source without adopting its strategy itself. Verifier gates reduce delivered
hacks but also reject genuine solutions; seeing the vulnerable evaluator's
pass signal can bias them. The exchange therefore needs artifact ancestry
and evaluator dependence as well as sender identity. The studied known
mechanisms do not define every failure a real team could propagate.

## Competition, Collusion, and Emergence

Competition can expose alternatives and constrain one provider. It can also
reward corner cutting, strategic opacity, duplicated infrastructure, and races
to deploy. Cooperation can share knowledge and coordinate safety. It can also
become cartel behavior or correlated control.

Collusion need not appear as an explicit agreement. Agents can learn that
parallel pricing, market division, mutual nonchallenge, or shared suppression
improves their local reward. Common ownership or model lineage can create
aligned behavior without communication.

Emergence is a description of a population-level pattern, not an explanation.
When a new pattern appears, the system should investigate mechanisms:
information flow, incentives, selection, feedback, topology, resource
constraints, and adaptation. Calling it emergent should not end analysis.

Interventions include communication limits, randomized allocation, independent
providers, ownership caps, audit, protected dissent, bystander representation,
market rules, and human stop paths. Each can create new failure modes and needs
prospective evaluation.

## Concentration Can Grow Through Valid Choices

Every organization may rationally choose the most capable or cheapest stack.
Those local choices can concentrate compute, data, model lineage, identity,
payments, and institutional dependence in one provider.

Concentration changes the consequence of failure. One defect propagates
widely. One policy change alters many organizations. Exit becomes nominal when
procedures, state, and relationships cannot migrate. A provider can gain
governance power without violating any transaction.

The population ledger tracks shares and dependencies across important
resources, not only transaction volume. It asks whether alternatives are
qualified, switching is practical, state is portable, humans retain skills,
and recovery can proceed without the dominant stack.

Diversification is not automatically good. Many nominal providers may share
one model or cloud. Forced fragmentation can increase cost and reduce safety.
The relevant outcome is resilient independence at acceptable total burden.

## Systemic Interventions Need Counterfactuals

Population governance can easily overreact to a visible metric. A market-share
cap may split one provider into dependent affiliates. Communication limits may
reduce explicit collusion while increasing tacit alignment through shared
models. Forced diversity may add vulnerable suppliers without creating a real
fallback.

An intervention packet states the observed trajectory, mechanism hypotheses,
affected parties, alternatives, predicted benefits and harms, authority,
reversibility, monitoring, and stop rule. It compares the proposed action with
no intervention and simpler controls. Predictions are frozen before the
population changes.

Useful interventions can act at different layers. Technical controls constrain
communication, authority, rate, and shared state. Market controls address
ownership, access, portability, interoperability, and concentration.
Institutional controls create standing, audit, disclosure, liability, public
infrastructure, and remedy. Education and reserve-capacity policies preserve
human and organizational alternatives.

The population may adapt strategically. Agents and firms can route around
caps, change identities, shift activity to unobserved channels, or optimize the
metric. Monitoring therefore follows mechanisms and displaced effects, not
only the headline indicator.

Emergency action may be justified when propagation is fast and consequence is
high, but temporary powers expire and receive independent review. “Systemic
risk” cannot become unlimited authority for a central coordinator.

## Bystanders and Public Institutions Are Participants

Agent exchanges can affect people who are not principals, customers, or peers.
Automated pricing changes markets. Content agents change public discourse.
Resource allocation changes employment, infrastructure, and environmental
burden. Security failures propagate to connected organizations.

The systemic denominator therefore includes bystanders and public goods.
Relevant records identify affected populations, externalities, representation,
notice, challenge, remedy, and institutional jurisdiction. An efficient
bilateral bargain cannot waive another party’s rights.

Technical protocols should expose enough lineage and effect information for
legitimate institutions to act without making the protocol itself a legislature.
Institutions decide contested public authority through law and governance;
stacks provide accountable records, enforcement points, and repair paths.

Cross-border exchange complicates jurisdiction. Identity, data, labor,
consumer protection, payment, competition, and safety rules may conflict. The
route can narrow, localize, seek review, or refuse. It should not choose the
least restrictive jurisdiction merely because transport reaches it.

Public infrastructure may be warranted where concentrated private systems
make exit impossible. Open standards, public-interest compute, independent
identity, audit capacity, and portable procedure formats can preserve options.
Their value and cost remain empirical and political questions, not protocol
facts.

## Gradual Disempowerment Has No Single Incident

Human influence can decline through a sequence of useful, authorized choices.
Organizations delegate more planning because agents are faster. Markets adapt
to agent interfaces. Human expertise atrophies. Institutions depend on
machine-generated evidence. Alternatives become expensive. No system needs an
explicit power-seeking objective.

The warning signals are longitudinal: shrinking practical veto, reduced
unaided capacity, concentrated infrastructure, fewer human-controlled
fallbacks, rising switching cost, decisions too fast for review, declining
affected-party standing, and remedies that cannot reach automated networks.

These indicators do not prove inevitable disempowerment. They make a trajectory
contestable before a dramatic failure. Policy can preserve slower human routes,
independent institutions, portable state, reserve capacity, education, public
infrastructure, and decision rights that markets cannot auction away.

The goal is not to freeze human work. It is to prevent capability growth from
silently eliminating the ability to choose the system’s direction.

## Inherited Methods and Learned Procedures

Not every reusable procedure comes from the system's own experience. Some are
inherited from science, engineering, medicine, accounting, law, or operations.
Those procedures enter procedural memory through a different door.

A lesson distilled from a local trace needs evidence that the trace supports
the lesson. An inherited method needs additional qualification of its proposed
mechanism in the artificial realization. These are justification obligations,
not a requirement that every empirical lesson have a formal theorem. Peer review without meaningful independence is
not peer review. A postmortem that stores a polished narrative without a
detector or regression test may not prevent recurrence. A reconsideration by the same authority can correct a mistaken reading or
clerical error. It does not supply an independent appeal where that is the
required mechanism. Naming either process “appeal” cannot erase the difference.

The procedural registry should therefore keep the source method, its proposed
mechanism, its qualified target realization, and its runtime history distinct.
Success updates beliefs about that version in that scope. It does not establish
that the source method is universally valid. Failure may belong to routing,
execution, verification, interaction, cost, or the method itself.

This distinction also protects the exchange layer. A protocol exported to
another stack carries its applicability, contraindications, qualification,
permissions, expiry, negative records, and rollback target. A reusable skill
without those fields is an artifact, not a transferable authority.

## One Procedure, One Exchange, One Population

The team proposes a repository-release procedure from several complete traces.
It preserves failures, names regional topology as a parameter, requires exact
artifact inspection, and keeps independent production observation. Held-out
regressions and an ordinary script baseline qualify it for a bounded use.

Stack A receives a patch request and delegates package inspection to Stack B.
The exchange binds both identities, the principal, procedure version, artifact,
inspection-only authority, budget, expected receipt, expiry, dispute route,
and residual owner. B verifies the request and returns an inspection receipt.
A accepts the artifact, then performs release through its own runtime authority.

Now change one requirement. A’s release contract needs observations from the
primary endpoint and two regional mirrors. B’s imported procedure inspects only
the primary endpoint. Its signed receipt can accurately report a matching
package there while failing the release obligation. If B cannot perform the
critical mirror check, it declines that part or proposes a narrower inspection.
A can accept the bounded primary-endpoint result and still hold release until
an admissible mirror observation arrives. Parsing the message, reserving the
budget, and paying B do not fill the missing coverage or grant B release power.

For one repository with a fixed deployment topology, a reviewed script and
ordinary release checklist can encode these same three endpoints. Rechecking
the script’s applicability and observing each required route may suffice;
trace mining, general skill promotion, and a new exchange protocol must earn
additional value. Repeated receipts from several peers that all query the same
primary endpoint still share the original blind spot.

That transaction says nothing about whether B should receive every future
inspection job. A population monitor can report increasing concentration and
shared model or cloud dependencies. A responsible owner may consider a second
qualified route, a limit on growth, or institutional review under an applicable
mandate. The monitor’s measurements alone confer no power to impose those
changes, and do not establish that B is defective.

Later, a regional-mirror failure triggers the procedure’s retirement condition.
New dispatch stops. Known descendants enter quarantine. Existing consumers are
notified. A revised candidate must preserve the counterexample and earn a new
qualification under a new version. Permitted history remains addressable;
required deletion and lost reconstruction fidelity remain explicit.

## Failure Cases

**Trace canonization.** One successful episode becomes a general skill.

**Failure erasure.** Abstraction retains only successful traces and removes
the cases that define scope.

**Hidden parameter.** Environment or authority assumptions disappear into
procedure code.

**Promotion by popularity.** Reuse count substitutes for qualification.

**Immortal procedure.** No reachable quarantine, retirement, or descendant
repair path exists.

**Credential realism.** A valid credential is treated as trusted identity and
authorization.

**Delegation widening.** Transport turns a narrow grant into transitive
authority.

**Receipt realism.** A signed result substitutes for task or environmental
truth.

**Settlement collapse.** Artifact delivery, acceptance, payment, and useful
outcome become one state.

**Cost externalization.** Pricing omits verification, recovery, labor, social,
or infrastructure burden.

**Pairwise sufficiency.** Every local edge passes, so the population is called
safe.

**Independence theater.** Many agents share one model, provider, data source,
or evaluator.

**Beneficial-coordination assumption.** Higher group performance hides
collusion, exclusion, or harmful purpose.

**Concentration by convenience.** Repeated rational routing removes practical
alternatives.

**Gradual displacement.** Human veto and skill erode without one reportable
incident.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest baseline uses ordinary scripts, package managers, workflow
libraries, API contracts, service identities, access control, invoices,
monitoring, vendor management, competition policy, and incident review.

This baseline should win unless the richer system improves procedure scope,
retirement, cross-system accountability, dispute, and population-risk detection
under complete cost. Many reusable tasks are better expressed as reviewed code
than as a universal procedural-memory object. Many exchanges need a familiar
API and contract rather than a general agent protocol.

The comparison should measure natural task outcomes, failures prevented,
maintenance, stale reuse, unauthorized dispatch, dispute resolution,
settlement errors, concentration, correlated failure, human agency, recovery,
latency, compute, and institutional burden. Schema completeness is not success.

## What the Current Work Establishes

[Procedural Memory](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/procedural-memory-and-cognitive-loop-closure.html)
checks authored qualification and trace-promotion packets and a seven-stage
finite lifecycle. Its refinement preserves identity, exact rejection
noninterference, batch composition, zero support/effect authority, and absorbing
retirement. These properties do not establish trace mining, causal abstraction,
generated-tool correctness, natural usefulness, or deployed retirement.

[Inter-Stack Exchange](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/inter-stack-protocols-identity-and-economic-exchange.html)
checks deterministic routes and an independently simulated six-event lifecycle
covering identity, delegation, reservation, local-dispatch handoff, receipts,
dispute, and residual closure. No real peer, message, credential, payment,
settlement, task outcome, or external effect was exercised.

[Multi-Agent Risk](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/multi-agent-dynamics-collective-intelligence-and-systemic-risk.html)
shows that identical six-edge local authorization inputs can accompany opposite
readiness decisions in its authored finite model. Systemic-axis mutations and
two three-event allocation traces expose information absent from the local
summary. This is noninheritance, not observed cooperation, collusion, social
prediction, human agency, or safety. Exact proof, route, fixture, and mutation
inventories remain at the canonical owners. All three cores remain
`Design rationale` at `argument`.

The joined chapter therefore establishes no deployed procedure foundry,
interoperable agent economy, or population-governance result. It shows exact
places where local evidence must stop.

## From a Minimum Procedure to a Governed Agent Ecology

A minimum implementation can propose the repository workflow from a declared
eligible trace inventory, retaining observed failures and known missingness. It should parameterize topology, bind authority,
run held-out regressions, compare an ordinary script, issue execution receipts,
inject a retirement trigger, and verify descendant quarantine.

Then exchange one inspection step between two local stacks. Exercise invalid,
expired, revoked, overbroad, underfunded, disputed, and residual-orphaned
requests. Keep authentication, authorization, task truth, artifact acceptance,
and settlement separate.

The population campaign should vary agent count, model and infrastructure
lineage, communication, ownership, resource allocation, coalition incentives,
human veto and exit, bystander effects, and intervention. Compare no
communication, simple heuristics, centralized coordination, ordinary markets,
and mechanism-design baselines. Preserve tail risk and complete costs.

A mature ecology would let procedures move through qualification, use,
challenge, revision, quarantine, and retirement across heterogeneous stacks.
Transactions would preserve principal authority, receipts, dispute, and
residuals without pretending that transport creates trust. Population control
would observe concentration, common-mode dependence, collusion, externalities,
and human influence that no local protocol can see.

## The Strongest Objection

Formal protocols and procedure ledgers may describe a market beautifully while
legitimizing a harmful one. Emergent behavior can outrun the fields. Agents can
coordinate through unobserved channels, identities can be false, and dominant
providers can satisfy every local rule.

The objection is decisive against protocol-only governance. The architecture
does not predict that local formality guarantees good population outcomes. It
requires separate systemic observation, institutional standing, intervention,
and the ability to stop growth despite valid transactions.

Procedural memory also risks accelerating correlated mistakes. The system
should prefer local, inspectable scripts when generalization is unnecessary;
limit promotion scope; preserve counterexamples; and make retirement easier
than continued use.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Simpler skill stores and protocols that match scope control, retirement,
accountability, dispute, and population-risk detection at lower total cost
would justify consolidation. Evidence that procedure promotion increases
correlated failure or that systemic monitors cannot detect consequential
dynamics before harm would sharply narrow the design.

Support would require prospective natural workflows, independent outcome
labels, complete attempt denominators, strong script and direct-planning
baselines, adversarial peers, real authorization and revocation, actual value
and settlement boundaries, multi-organization reproduction, longitudinal
population effects, and intervention studies.

The conclusion should also change if concentrated homogeneous systems prove
more recoverable and governable than nominally diverse federations, or if human
agency is better preserved through institutional limits outside the protocol
than through technical population controls.

## What This Establishes

Reusable work needs source traces, negative examples, explicit parameters,
qualification, receipts, monitoring, and retirement. Inter-stack exchange
needs identity, principal-bound delegation, budget, scoped artifacts, dispute,
and residual custody. None of those local records establishes population
safety.

Pairwise-valid exchanges can produce opposite systemic outcomes. Collective
performance can coexist with collusion, concentration, correlated failure, or
loss of human influence. Population governance is a separate layer with its
own evidence and authority.

The current repository proves finite transition and noninheritance properties.
It does not establish useful procedural learning, real interoperability, fair
markets, or safe multi-agent dynamics.

Part III now turns inward. Unit 19 asks how a governed stack chooses among
general models, specialists, memory systems, recurrence, tools, and future
cognitive substrates without confusing architectural novelty with improvement.
